name: Seshapureeswarar Temple, Tirupampuram
deity: Shiva as Seshapureeswarar (Paampuranathar, lord of the serpents)
tradition: Shaiva — a Paadal Petra Sthalam, sung by Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar
summary: Tirupampuram, near Kuthalam, is a Paadal Petra Sthalam where Shiva is worshipped as Seshapureeswarar — also Paampuranathar, lord of the serpents — and which is famed as a centre for Rahu–Ketu and naga-dosha remedies. By tradition, when Shiva cursed the serpent race for its pride, the nagas — among them Adisesha, Rahu and Ketu — were released by worshipping him here on Maha Shivaratri. Sung by Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar, it is the third of the four Naga temples of a one-day circuit.

sections.history: Tirupampuram, near Kuthalam in the Kaveri delta, is an ancient Shaiva village hymned in the seventh-century Tevaram by all three principal saints — Sambandar, Appar and Sundarar — and counted among the Paadal Petra Sthalams. Its historical names, Paampuram and Seshapuri, carry its deep association with the serpents, the nagas, and the stone temple of the Chola period has become, in modern times, a much-sought centre for remedies against serpent-related afflictions.
sections.architecture: The temple follows the Dravidian plan with a gopuram, prakara and the sanctum of Seshapureeswarar. Its devotional life centres on the nagas: the shrines and images connected with Adisesha, Rahu and Ketu are the focus of the special worship for which the temple is known. The serpent motif runs through its iconography, marking it among the delta temples where naga-worship is pre-eminent.
sections.legends: The great legend of Tirupampuram concerns the pride of the serpents. In one telling, as Ganesha worshipped Shiva on Mount Kailasa, the serpent coiled about the lord's neck wrongly took the worship as its own and grew arrogant; angered, Shiva cursed the whole serpent race to lose its powers. The nagas, pleading that all should not suffer for one, were told to worship him on the night of Maha Shivaratri, and Adisesha led them — to Kumbakonam, Tirunageswaram, Nagore and finally Tirupampuram — until their curse was lifted. From this the temple became a powerful centre for Rahu–Ketu and naga-dosha remedies, sought by those facing such doshas or childlessness.
sections.festivals: Maha Shivaratri is the temple's foremost festival, carrying the memory of the night the serpents were redeemed, and it draws great crowds. The regular Shaiva observances of Pradosham and the Margazhi season are kept, and devotees often make a same-day circuit of the four Naga temples, of which Tirupampuram is the third. Special worship for Rahu and Ketu is offered through the year.
sections.experience: Tirupampuram draws pilgrims who come with a particular prayer — for relief from naga-dosha, for Rahu–Ketu remedies, for children. The darshan of Seshapureeswarar, the lord of the serpents, carries the sense of a grace that lifted an ancient curse, and for many the temple is a place of hope at a difficult turn of life.

visit.timings: Typically open from early morning to midday and again from late afternoon into the evening; confirm timings locally, especially on festival days.
visit.dressCode: Modest traditional attire is expected, with shoulders and knees covered; footwear is left at the entrance.
visit.photography: Photography is generally allowed in the outer corridors but not inside the sanctum; ask temple staff before photographing rituals.
visit.gettingThere: Tirupampuram is in Tiruvarur district near Kuthalam, roughly 15 km from Mayiladuthurai; the nearest rail heads are Kuthalam and Mayiladuthurai, with local buses and taxis to the village. It is often visited with the other three Naga temples (Kumbakonam, Tirunageswaram, Nagore).
